entry: Landlocked state in the Mountain West subregion of the [[Western United States]], bordered by [[Idaho]], [[Wyoming]] and three Canadian provinces. It is the fourth-largest state by area but the eighth-least populous. Its capital is Helena, and its largest city is Billings. Most of the territory came under American sovereignty with the [[Louisiana Purchase]] from France in 1803, and statehood followed on November 8, 1889. [[Mining]] was the main economic engine until the mid-20th century. The economy rests on [[Agriculture|agriculture]], including ranching and cereal grain farming, with oil, gas, coal and lumber also significant. Tourism is the fastest-growing sector, with 13.7 million visitors in 2024.

Quarter and ward of [[Monaco]] on the French Riviera, synonymous with [[Gambling|gambling]] and luxury. The first casino opened in La Condamine in 1862 but was unsuccessful, and it relocated several times before reaching its present site in the Les Spélugues area. A railway installed in 1868 brought visitors, and the town grew in wealth. Its narrow street circuit has hosted the [[Formula One|Monaco Grand Prix]] since 1929. The ward has about 3,500 permanent residents and the quarter about 15,000.

Class of computational algorithms based on repeated random sampling, conceived by Polish mathematician Stanisław Ulam. The method uses randomness to solve deterministic problems. It is mainly used for optimization, [[Numerical integration|numerical integration]] and generating non-uniform random variates, and it models phenomena with large input uncertainties, such as risk assessments for nuclear power plants. It is applied in physics, chemistry, finance and cryptography. The name refers to the Monte Carlo Casino in [[Monaco]], inspired by Ulam's uncle's gambling habits.

Country on the [[Balkans|Balkan Peninsula]] in Southeastern Europe, with a coastline on the [[Adriatic Sea]]. Its 25 municipalities had a total population of 633,158. The capital and largest city is Podgorica, while Cetinje is the old royal capital and cultural center. After Ottoman rule, Montenegro gained semi-autonomy in 1696 under the House of Petrović-Njegoš, first as a theocracy and later as a secular principality. Its independence was recognized at the [[Congress of Berlin]] in 1878, and it became a kingdom in 1910. After World War I it became part of [[Yugoslavia]], and after that state broke up it formed a federation with Serbia. Montenegro declared independence in June 2006 following a referendum. It is a member of the [[United Nations]], [[NATO]] and the [[World Trade Organization]], and has been in the process of joining the [[European Union]] since 2012. Its upper-middle-income economy is mostly service-based, with tourism contributing around 30 percent of GDP.

Capital and largest city of the northeastern Mexican state of Nuevo León, at the foothills of the Sierra Madre Oriental. Diego de Montemayor founded the city on September 20, 1596, and it grew into a key business hub after the [[Mexican War of Independence]]. The Monterrey Foundry, established in 1900, spurred industrial growth. The city holds prominent positions in industries such as [[Steel|steel]], cement, glass, auto parts and brewing, and it is the biggest industrial city in [[Mexico]]. The city proper had 1,142,194 residents, making it Mexico's eighth-largest city. It is home to the Monterrey Institute of Technology and Higher Education, the largest private university in Mexico. Its economic success has been partly attributed to its proximity to the United States border.

French jurist, historian and political philosopher. He is the principal source of the theory of [[Separation of powers|separation of powers]], which many [[Constitution|constitutions]] implement, and he propagated the term despotism in modern political thought. Born at the Château de La Brède, south of [[Bordeaux]], he inherited the office of président à mortier in the Bordeaux Parlement in 1716 and sold it in 1726. His satirical *Persian Letters* (1721), which portrays French society through two Persian visitors, was an instant classic. He was elected to the Académie Française in 1728. His anonymously published *De l'esprit des lois* (1748; *The Spirit of Law*) was well received in Great Britain and the American colonies, and it influenced the Founding Fathers in drafting the U.S. Constitution.

Child-centered teaching method that encourages self-directed learning. Italian physician [[Maria Montessori]] began developing it in 1897, and her first classroom, the Casa dei Bambini, opened in a tenement in [[Rome]] in 1907. Montessori classrooms emphasize hands-on learning, mixed-age groups, student autonomy in choosing topics, long uninterrupted work periods, specially trained teachers and a prepared environment, and they generally avoid grades and tests. The name is not trademarked, so practices vary widely. Scientific studies generally report favorable outcomes for students.

Capital and largest city of [[Uruguay]], on the northeastern bank of the [[Río de la Plata]]. The city proper had 1,287,452 residents at the 2023 census, about 36.8 percent of the national population. A Portuguese garrison was established on the site in November 1723 and expelled in February 1724 by the Spanish soldier Bruno Mauricio de Zabala. The foundation date of December 24, 1726 comes from Zabala's diary, as no official document records it. The city is the seat of the headquarters of Mercosur and ALADI, Latin America's leading trade blocs. The 2019 Mercer report rated it first in Latin America for quality of life, a rank it has held since 2005. Montevideo hosted every match of the first [[FIFA World Cup]] in 1930, and it is one of the cities with the most [[Art Deco]] influence. It is the country's chief port and financial center.

French inventors and aviation pioneers, and paper manufacturers from Annonay. Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier developed the [[Hot air balloon|hot-air balloon]] in 1782 and 1783. Their balloon, the *Globe aérostatique*, carried Jacques-Étienne on the first confirmed piloted human ascent in 1783. Joseph-Michel had built [[Parachute|parachutes]] as early as 1775, and later invented the self-acting hydraulic ram (1796). Jacques-Étienne founded the first paper-making vocational school. Together the brothers invented a process for manufacturing transparent paper. Born into a family of paper manufacturers in Annonay, Étienne had trained as an architect in Paris before running the family mills. Joseph-Michel's first experiments, in 1782, used a lightweight wooden box covered in taffeta, which rose when paper was lit beneath it.

Capital city of the U.S. state of [[Alabama]] and county seat of Montgomery County, on the Alabama River. It was named for Continental Army major general Richard Montgomery and incorporated in 1819. The city had 200,603 residents at the 2020 census. In February 1861 it was chosen as the first capital of the [[Confederate States of America]], until the government moved to [[Richmond, Virginia]] that May. In the mid-20th century Montgomery was a major center of the [[Civil rights movement]], including the Montgomery bus boycott and the Selma to Montgomery marches. Maxwell Air Force Base and Hyundai Motor Manufacturing Alabama are major employers.

American actor known for portraying sensitive, moody young men. A four-time Academy Award nominee, he was among the first actors invited to study at the Actors Studio with [[Elia Kazan]]. Along with [[Marlon Brando]] and [[James Dean]], he was considered one of the original method actors in Hollywood, though he distanced himself from the term. His films include *Red River* (1948), *A Place in the Sun* (1951), *From Here to Eternity* (1953) and *The Misfits* (1961). A car crash in 1956 severely injured his face and worsened his struggles with alcohol and prescription drugs.

Unit of time, used with calendars, that is approximately as long as a cycle of the [[Moon|Moon]]'s phases. The synodic month, from one new moon to the next, averages 29.53059 days, so there are roughly 12.37 such months in one Earth year. Calendars that developed from the Roman system, such as the [[Gregorian calendar]], divide the year into 12 months of 28 to 31 days. The names of months 9 to 12 come from Latin numerals 7 to 10, because they were originally the seventh through tenth months of the Roman calendar. In the Gregorian calendar only February varies, with 29 days in a [[Leap year|leap year]] and 28 otherwise. Astronomers also recognize the sidereal month, about 27.32166 days, and the anomalistic month, about 27.55455 days.

Largest city in the province of [[Quebec]], Canada, and the second-largest in the country. Founded in 1642 as Ville-Marie, it takes its name from Mount Royal, the triple-peaked hill around which the early settlement grew. The 2021 census recorded 1,762,949 residents in the city and 4,291,732 in the metropolitan area, the second-largest in Canada after [[Toronto]]. French is the official language, and Montreal is the largest primarily French-speaking city in the Americas. Historically the commercial capital of Canada, it was surpassed by Toronto in the 1970s. It is the headquarters of the International Civil Aviation Organization and was named a [[UNESCO]] City of Design in 2006. Montreal hosted Expo 67 and the 1976 Summer Olympics, the only Canadian city to host the Games. It also hosts the Canadian Grand Prix of [[Formula One|Formula One]] and is home to the Canadiens of the [[National Hockey League]].

Professional [[Ice hockey|ice hockey]] team based in [[Montreal]], colloquially known as the Habs. Founded in 1909, the Canadiens are the oldest continuously operating professional ice hockey team in the world and the only existing [[National Hockey League]] club to predate the league. The franchise was one of the Original Six teams in the NHL from 1942 until the 1967 expansion. The Canadiens have won the Stanley Cup 24 times, more than any other franchise. Their championship season of 1992–93 was the last time a Canadian team won the Stanley Cup. It has played at the Bell Centre since 1996.

British Overseas Territory in the [[Caribbean]], part of the [[Lesser Antilles]]. The [[Volcano|Soufrière Hills volcano]] became active on July 18, 1995, and its eruptions destroyed Plymouth, the capital, on the west coast. About two-thirds of the population fled, mostly to the [[United Kingdom]]. An exclusion zone covers the southern part of the island because of [[Pyroclastic flow|pyroclastic]] flow hazards. The population had risen to nearly 5,000 by 2016. In June 2022 work began on a new town and port at Little Bay, a £28 million project funded by the UK and the Caribbean Development Bank.

Probability puzzle based on the American game show *Let's Make a Deal* and named after its host, Monty Hall. A contestant picks one of three doors, behind one of which is a car, and the host opens a door hiding a goat. Should the contestant switch? Marilyn vos Savant answered in her Ask Marilyn column in *Parade* in 1990 that switching gives a 2/3 chance of winning. About 10,000 readers, including nearly 1,000 with PhDs, wrote in, most calling her wrong. Simulations and formal proofs confirm her answer. The solution is counterintuitive, which makes the problem a [[Paradox|paradox]], and it illustrates [[Bayes' theorem]].

British surreal comedy troupe, formed in 1969 by Graham Chapman, John Cleese, Terry Gilliam, Eric Idle, Terry Jones and Michael Palin. Their sketch series *Monty Python's Flying Circus* aired on the [[BBC]] from 1969 to 1974, and it pushed the boundaries of television comedy through a stream-of-consciousness approach and Gilliam's animation. The troupe then made the films *Monty Python and the Holy Grail* (1975), *Life of Brian* (1979) and *The Meaning of Life* (1983). In 1988 they received the BAFTA Award for Outstanding British Contribution to Cinema, and in 1998 the AFI Star Award. Their influence on comedy has been compared to that of [[The Beatles|the Beatles]] on music.

Group of mental and behavioral disorders in which the main underlying characteristic is a disturbance of mood, also known as an affective disorder. They are classified in the DSM and ICD. Mood disorders include abnormally elevated mood, such as [[Mania|mania]] or hypomania, and depressed mood, the best-known form of which is [[Major depressive disorder]]. [[Bipolar disorder]] cycles between mania and depression, and milder subtypes include [[Dysthymia|dysthymic disorder]] and cyclothymic disorder. Some mood disorders are substance-induced or occur in response to a medical condition. Epidemiological studies in Europe suggest that roughly 8.5 percent of the world's population has a depressive disorder. People with major depression are at increased risk of [[Suicide|suicide]], and treatment dramatically reduces that risk.

Affective state that is less specific and less intense than an [[Emotion|emotion]] and less likely to be provoked by a particular event. Moods are typically positive or negative in valence, as in being in a good or bad mood. They are shorter-lived than temperament or personality traits, although traits such as optimism and neuroticism predispose certain moods. Long-term disturbances, such as [[Depression (mood)|clinical depression]] and [[Bipolar disorder|bipolar disorder]], are considered mood disorders. Positive mood has been found to enhance creative problem solving, though it can also disrupt performance when distracting information is present. The English word derives from Old English mōd, which denoted military courage as well as temper or disposition.

Fictional family of white, round, hippo-like trolls created by the [[Finland|Finnish]] writer and illustrator Tove Jansson. The Moomins live in Moominvalley. Between 1945 and 1993 Jansson wrote nine books about them, five picture books and a long-running comic strip. The first two books, published in 1945 and 1946, dealt with natural disasters and were influenced by the upheavals of war. The characters have inspired television series, films, theatre, video games and theme parks, and a Japanese animated series from 1990 to 1992. The Moomins also appear on merchandise, and on some Finnair aircraft as a livery.

Arrival of a crewed or robotic lander on the [[Moon]]. The first human-made object to touch the Moon was the Soviet Luna 2 in 1959, a hard landing. The first soft landing was Luna 9 in 1966. The first crewed landing was [[Apollo 11]] in July 1969, when [[Neil Armstrong]] and [[Buzz Aldrin]] reached the surface. Six crewed landings followed between 1969 and 1972 under the [[Apollo program|Apollo program]], and twelve astronauts have landed on the Moon. Five nations, the [[Soviet Union]], the United States, China, India and Japan, have achieved soft robotic landings. China's Chang'e 4 made the first landing on the [[Far side of the Moon|far side]] in 2019. India's Chandrayaan-3 landed in the lunar south polar region in August 2023.

Natural satellites of [[Jupiter]], a system of 115 known moons as of April 9, 2026. The four Galilean moons, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, were discovered in 1610 by [[Galileo Galilei]] and Simon Marius. They were the first objects found to orbit a body other than Earth or the Sun. Each is over 3,100 km in diameter, and all other Jovian moons are under 250 km. Eight regular satellites orbit close to Jupiter's equatorial plane. The outer irregular moons, which have inclined and eccentric orbits, were probably captured as [[Asteroid|asteroids]] or formed from their fragments.

Phobos and Deimos, the two small, irregularly shaped natural satellites of [[Mars]]. American astronomer Asaph Hall discovered both in August 1877. They are named after the sons of Ares, who accompanied their father into battle. Phobos is 22.2 km across and orbits at a semi-major axis of 9,377 km, while [[Deimos (moon)|Deimos]] is 12.6 km across and orbits at 23,460 km. Two hypotheses remain: that the moons formed from Mars after a giant impact, or that they are captured asteroids. Sample return missions may distinguish between them. [[Jonathan Swift]] had described two Martian moons in *Gulliver's Travels* (1726), more than a century before their discovery.

Natural satellites of [[Neptune]], with 16 known moons. The largest, [[Triton (moon)|Triton]], was discovered by William Lassell on October 10, 1846, seventeen days after Neptune itself. Triton orbits in the retrograde direction, opposite to the planet's rotation, which suggests it was captured rather than formed in orbit around Neptune. Its capture disrupted the original moons, which collided to form a rubble disc. Seven small inner moons, Neptune's only regular satellites, were re-accreted from that disc. Eight outer irregular satellites orbit farther out. [[Voyager 2]] flew past Neptune in 1989, recovering Larissa and discovering five inner moons.

Natural satellites of [[Saturn]], which has 293 confirmed moons as of June 2026, the most of any planet. [[Titan (moon)|Titan]], larger than the planet [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]], is the second-largest moon in the Solar System. It has a nitrogen-rich atmosphere and landscapes with river networks and hydrocarbon lakes. [[Enceladus]] emits jets of ice from its south polar region. Twenty-five moons are regular satellites with mostly prograde orbits, while the 268 irregular moons are probably captured minor planets or their fragments. The largest irregular moon, Phoebe, is named for a Greek Titaness. [[Christiaan Huygens]] identified Titan in 1655.
